title: Farmer's soil probe: replica-leakage sensor triggers refresh per mat
idea: A farmer irrigates when the soil probe reads dry, not by the calendar. Each 512-row mat gets a 'probe' of 256 minimum-Vt, maximum-GIDL replica access transistors in parallel discharging a 50 fF reference node; a comparator fires that mat's refresh when the replica node crosses the sense limit, so the interval follows real temperature, voltage and aging instead of the 85 C worst case.
why: Refresh (fact 3): servers typically run at 40-60 C, where retention is 4-16x the spec point; a tracking interval cuts refresh energy and lost bandwidth 3-8x for ~0.1% probe area.

title: Child's empty cups: minority-charge encoding with zero-row refresh skip
idea: A child notes that empty cups cannot spill. Each 64-bit word is stored with one invert bit chosen so at most half its cells sit in the charged (leak-prone) state, respecting true-cell/anti-cell polarity; a per-row 'all-safe' flag set on write lets the refresh engine skip rows that hold only discharged states.
why: Retention failures come only from charged cells: halving them halves tail exposure, and zero-filled or sparse rows (often 20-40% of server pages) skip refresh entirely; ~1.5-2.5x refresh energy cut for ~1.6% storage overhead.

title: EV power engineer's SiC access tier bonded beneath the capacitors
idea: An EV inverter engineer reaches for 4H-SiC, now mass-produced on 200 mm wafers for cars, including in U.S. fabs. Build high-temperature-activated SiC access MOSFETs first, layer-transfer the 1 um SiC film onto the DRAM wafer, then build capacitors above; SiC's intrinsic carrier density (~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 for Si) removes thermal generation as a leakage path.
why: Junction and generation leakage drop by many decades, pushing retention from 64 ms toward minutes, so refresh (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) nearly vanishes; low SiC mobility is acceptable for an access switch.

title: Biologist's DNA proofreading: early-warning margin reads before cells fail
idea: Cells repair DNA lesions before they become mutations. A background scrubber reads each row with the sense-amp reference deliberately shifted ~30% of signal toward the decayed level; rows whose ECC syndrome changes under the shifted read are flagged 'damaged' and refreshed now, while rows that stay clean have their own refresh period doubled step by step, up to 1 s.
why: Refresh is set by the worst row at the worst temperature; evidence-based per-row periods cut refresh operations 4-10x and catch variable-retention cells as they shift.

title: Embargoed Soviet tube engineer: vacuum-nanogap field-emission access switch
idea: Soviet designers kept vacuum tubes in the MiG-25 because they shrugged off radiation. Put the storage node behind a sealed 10-20 nm vacuum cavity facing a sharp metal emitter tip; the wordline gate raises the tip field to switch on field-emission current, and with the gate low the gap has no carriers, no junction and no trap states to leak through.
why: Off-state leakage, set by Fowler-Nordheim emission at low field, is effectively zero (<1e-21 A), removing refresh; it is also radiation-hard and needs no high-purity crystalline channel.

title: Venusian alien's diamond access transistors for hot, chiller-free memory
idea: An alien from 460 C Venus would never cool its memory. Grow boron-delta-doped or hydrogen-terminated diamond (5.5 eV gap) thin-film access FETs by low-temperature plasma CVD over the capacitors; leakage stays sub-fA even at 150-200 C, so DRAM can sit hot beside accelerators.
why: Today refresh doubles every ~10 C, which forces cooling; diamond access devices hold retention at 150 C, cutting refresh to near zero and removing memory-side chiller energy, and diamond needs only carbon.

title: 2050 engineer's hBN-sealed WSe2 access channel with vdW contacts
idea: A 2050 engineer would wonder why we ever used channels with dangling bonds. Transfer a monolayer WSe2 or MoS2 channel, fully encapsulated top and bottom in hBN, onto the capacitor tops and contact it with van der Waals-transferred metal, so there are no doped junctions or pinning defects; leakage is bounded by the 1.6-2 eV gap and atomically clean interfaces.
why: Removes the junction/trap-assisted-tunneling tail behind the 13 fA spec (fact 3); projected off-current <1e-19 A per cell gives seconds-to-minutes retention, and a 0.7 nm body suppresses DIBL so channels can shorten (density).

title: Dam engineer's spillway: resonant-tunneling barriers isolate the storage node
idea: A dam spillway passes water only above a set level. Replace the access channel with a double-barrier quantum-well stack (AlN/GaN/AlN or SiO2/Si-well/SiO2) between bitline and storage node; the wordline shifts the well's subband into resonance for fast transfer, while off-resonance transmission through two barriers is exponentially suppressed.
why: On/off ratios of 1e15 or more with no doped junction remove refresh, and transfer happens at ~1 V; extends the UltraRAM barrier idea to DRAM speed and endurance.

title: Plumber's pressure equalization: well bias idles the storage junction
idea: A plumber knows no pressure difference means no leak. During idle, the bank's p-well is raised ~0.4 V and the cell plate shifted to preserve stored levels, so the storage-node junction sees near-zero reverse bias and the field-enhanced trap-assisted tunneling behind the leakage tail collapses; both are restored a few ns before any activation.
why: The weak-cell tail is trap-assisted tunneling and GIDL, exponentially field-dependent: cutting peak junction field ~40% can raise tail retention 4-10x and cut idle/self-refresh power, today 16-33% of idle.

title: Kintsugi artist: in-field electro-thermal anneal heals variable-retention cells
idea: Kintsugi repairs the crack instead of discarding the bowl. When the scrubber finds a variable-retention cell, the controller fires a burst of high-current pulses through that cell's access device to Joule-heat the junction to ~400 C for microseconds, releasing hydrogen from an adjacent hydrogen-rich SiN liner that repassivates the trap.
why: VRT cells set the refresh interval (fact 3) and are remapped or scrapped; in-situ healing shrinks the tail over life, letting refresh periods double or more and recovering yield.

title: Astronomer's standard star: co-decaying ghost reference cells per row
idea: Astronomers correct for haze with a reference star in the same frame. Every row holds two ghost cells written at mid-charge whenever the row is written or refreshed; they leak alongside the data, and the sense amp uses their decayed level as the reference instead of a fixed VBL/2, so data stays readable after much more decay.
why: A fixed reference loses margin as stored '1's sag; a co-decaying reference roughly doubles to quadruples usable retention, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth 2-4x for <1% area.

title: Banker's insured deposits: refresh-free banks for data with backups
idea: A banker guards insured deposits lightly because losses are covered. Pages with a valid copy elsewhere (model weights, page cache, read-only datasets) go into banks run with refresh off or at 1-4 s, protected by strong per-line detection codes; a detected error triggers a transparent refetch from flash, CXL or a remote replica instead of a crash.
why: Read-mostly AI weights are a large share of DRAM; dropping their refresh cuts refresh power and bandwidth 50-90% in those banks with only detection metadata added.

title: Sushi chef's freshness window: refresh-free ephemeral memory with expiry
idea: A sushi chef never stores fish past its window; it is served fresh. A new 'ephemeral' allocation class for activations, KV scratch and network buffers stamps each row with its write time; those rows are never refreshed, and the controller traps any read after the guaranteed retention window (e.g., 32 ms at the measured temperature) so software recomputes.
why: AI activations live microseconds to milliseconds; skipping refresh on them reclaims the 10-20% refresh bandwidth tax at high densities for the most bandwidth-hungry data.

title: Watchmaker's escapement: tunnel-diode Goto pair keeps cells latched
idea: An escapement gives a pendulum a tiny kick each swing so it never stops. Stack two nanoscale Esaki tunnel diodes (a Goto pair) on each storage node between plate rails; their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages sustained by pA valley current, so charge is continuously restored with no refresh at near-1T cell area.
why: Eliminates refresh (fact 3) at perhaps 1.3-1.5x cell area versus ~20x for 6T SRAM; standby stays ~pA per cell if the diode peak-to-valley ratio is high.

title: Glassblower's indium-free amorphous Ga2O3 ultra-wide-gap access channel
idea: A glassblower knows amorphous networks forgive disorder. Instead of indium-based IGZO, deposit ALD amorphous Ga2O3 or AlGaOx at <400 C as a back-end access channel; its ~4.8 eV gap pushes off-current toward 1e-22 A per cell and it avoids indium, a byproduct metal concentrated in China.
why: Retention of hours removes refresh and lets capacitors shrink, and frees oxide-semiconductor DRAM from indium supply risk (scarce-resource axis).

title: Locksmith's deadbolt: separate per-row hold gate on vertical channels
idea: A locksmith throws the deadbolt only when the house is empty. Each vertical access pillar gets a second gate on its back face, tied per row: idle rows hold it at -1.5 V for a very high threshold, and it is released to 0 V ~2 ns before that row activates, so the front wordline needs no negative off level and its GIDL disappears.
why: Separates 'hold' from 'switch': ~0.3 V higher idle threshold (about 5 decades less subthreshold leakage) without the GIDL penalty, cutting refresh ~5-10x and permitting a lower wordline high level.

title: Heavy-water reactor engineer: deuterium-cured access transistor interfaces
idea: A CANDU operator has tonnes of heavy water on hand. Replace the final forming-gas anneal with a 10-20 atm deuterium anneal so Si/SiO2 and junction dangling bonds are capped with Si-D bonds, which resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation ~10x better than Si-H and so stop traps from growing into variable-retention cells over life.
why: Narrows the end-of-life leakage tail, letting refresh intervals relax ~1.5-3x and improving yield; deuterium comes from Canada and the U.S., not a chokepoint.

title: Mechanic's torque wrench: per-row fused negative wordline level
idea: A mechanic torques each bolt to its own spec. At test, each row's leakiest cell is measured and a 3-bit fuse sets that row's off-level from 0 to -0.6 V, applied by its local sub-wordline drivers; strong rows sit near 0 V (low GIDL, low stress) and only weak rows get deep negative bias.
why: A single global negative wordline trades subthreshold leakage against GIDL; tuning per row lifts worst-case retention ~2-4x and reduces the large wordline swings that aggravate row hammer.

title: Wine merchant's vintages: retention-binned DRAM dies sold by grade
idea: Wine is sold by vintage, not poured away for missing Grand Cru. Test every die at 32/64/128/256 ms retention and sell grades: long-retention dies at a premium for phones and laptops, and dies that fail 64 ms (scrapped or heavily repaired today) as 'short-retention' parts run at 16 ms refresh in cache-like or CXL-pool roles.
why: Raises usable supply by recovering dies lost to the retention tail (several % yield) and earns a premium on long-retention dies for low-power markets.

title: Gardener's graft: transistor-last access devices on transferred crystal silicon
idea: A gardener grafts a healthy scion onto rootstock. Build the capacitor array first at its full thermal budget, then bond and smart-cut a pristine 50 nm single-crystal Si layer on top and form access transistors at <=500 C with in-situ-doped, laser-activated junctions, so no capacitor anneal ever crosses the junctions and no implant damage seeds traps.
why: Implant damage and thermal cycling seed the leakage tail; a damage-free low-thermal-budget junction could improve tail retention 3-10x, and decoupling capacitor and transistor processes also eases the 3D DRAM blocker (fact 2).

title: Hermit crab's borrowed shell: re-screen retired DIMMs at faster refresh
idea: A hermit crab moves into a used shell. Hyperscaler-retired DDR4/DDR5 modules are bulk-tested hot for retention, re-binned, and redeployed behind CXL memory expanders that run them at 2-4x refresh rate with stronger ECC as pooled cold-tier memory.
why: Adds usable memory without new wafers; extra refresh compensates for aged retention tails. Even a few % of the retired fleet is a large supply in a 4x price spike.

title: Building inspector's occupancy certificate: per-bank retention data in SPD
idea: An inspector certifies each room's safe occupancy. A JEDEC rule, seeded by CHIPS Act procurement, requires every module's SPD to store measured per-bank retention at three temperatures from final test, and DRAM to expose per-bank refresh-rate registers, so the OS and controller refresh each bank at its own rate instead of the global worst case.
why: Most banks retain 4-16x longer than the worst bank; standardized data unlocks ~2-4x refresh savings across the installed base with firmware, not fabs.

title: Innkeeper's rule: house the restless guests in the weak rows
idea: An innkeeper puts the up-all-night guests in the rooms by the noisy street. The controller profiles weak rows and remaps the hottest pages (touched more often than every 16 ms) into them, since every activation restores charge; strong rows hold cold data, and the global refresh period is set by strong rows only.
why: Turns natural activations into free refresh: the global interval can stretch 2-4x, with a fallback refresh only when a weak row goes quiet.

title: Titan alien's 77 K memory pool with sub-volt wordlines
idea: An alien from 94 K Titan would run memory where its physics is happiest. Pooled DRAM is immersed in liquid nitrogen and the array redesigned for 77 K: subthreshold slope steepens to ~20 mV/dec, so the access threshold drops and the wordline swings 0.8 V instead of a pumped 3 V, VARY falls to ~0.5 V, and leakage-driven refresh disappears.
why: Wordline and array CV^2 plus pump losses fall ~10-20x per access and refresh energy goes to ~0; the cryocooler cost (~5-10 W per W removed) only pays off for large shared pools, so the device-level gain must be big.

title: Pendulum maker's LC-resonant wordlines recycle their own swing
idea: A pendulum keeps swinging because energy trades between height and speed. Each bank's wordline drivers share an interposer inductor that forms an LC tank with the selected wordline's capacitance; the wordline rises and falls on a sinusoid and its charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground, with the pump only topping up losses.
why: A ~3 V wordline fed by ~30%-efficient pumps is a large share of activate energy (fact 10); 85-90% recovery with no pump loss cuts wordline energy ~10x per access.

title: Librarian fetches one book: row-and-column coincident access cell
idea: A librarian pulls one book, not the whole shelf. Each cell gets a second vertical access transistor in series, gated by a column-group select line, so a cell reaches its bitline only when both its row and its 64-bit group are selected; the other 127/128 of the row stay isolated, unread and unrestored.
why: Removes the 128x overfetch and the destructive restore of untouched cells (fact 8): activate energy per useful bit drops ~10-50x and row-hammer disturb shrinks; costs ~1.3-1.5x cell area unless the second device is stacked vertically.

title: Firefighters' bucket brigade: CCD charge transfer replaces long bitlines
idea: A bucket brigade passes water hand to hand instead of filling a long pipe. Cells line a buried-channel CCD column; on access, the selected cell dumps its packet into the CCD, low-swing three-phase clocks walk it ~32 stages to a floating-diffusion sense node at the mat edge, and it is walked back to rewrite, so no long bitline is ever charged.
why: Only the signal packet (~10k electrons) moves, at low clock swing, instead of a ~50-100 fF bitline per bit, cutting array energy per access ~10x; revives 1970s CCD memory with modern image-sensor transfer efficiency (>99.999%).

title: Child's whisper: +/-100 mV storage with auto-zeroed sense amps
idea: A child asks why memory shouts when a whisper carries. Store bits as +/-100 mV around the mid level instead of 0/1.1 V with bitlines parked at mid; chopper/auto-zero sense amplifiers cancel their own offsets to <3 mV each cycle, and a low-Vt access device suffices because the storage node always sits near the bitline potential.
why: Array energy scales as C*V^2: cutting the swing from 1.1 V to 0.2 V lowers cell and bitline energy ~10-30x per access, and the tiny hold Vds also cuts leakage.

title: Electric eel's stacked cells: voltage-stacked subarrays reuse one charge
idea: An electric eel stacks thousands of low-voltage cells in series. Four subarrays sit in a series voltage stack across a 2.2 V rail, each in its own 0.55 V domain, so charge one subarray draws while sensing flows on as the next one's supply; a small push-pull regulator balances mismatched activity.
why: Each supply coulomb is used four times (~4x) and the low per-domain swing cuts CV^2 (~2.5x), together ~10x lower energy per access from the rail, with less current delivery and IR loss.

title: Archer's drawn bow: pre-stressed NEMS relay access at 0.2 V
idea: A drawn bow releases great energy at a finger's touch. Each access device is a lateral nanoelectromechanical relay whose beam is built pre-stressed near snap-through (a negative-stiffness bistable flexure), so a 0.2 V gate nudge closes the contact; open, it is an air gap with zero leakage.
why: Zero off-current removes refresh, and a 0.2 V actuation versus a 3 V wordline is ~200x less gate CV^2; key risks are 1e15-cycle contact endurance and ns-scale closing.

title: Geologist's squeezed crystal: piezoelectronic access transistor
idea: A geologist knows squeezing certain crystals turns insulators into metals. Each access switch is a piezoelectronic transistor: a thin PMN-PT actuator driven at ~0.15 V compresses a SmSe pressure-driven insulator-metal layer between bitline and storage node, switching it in acoustic-transit time, with a wide-gap blocking layer in series to reach DRAM-grade off-resistance.
why: A 0.1-0.2 V gate versus a 3 V pumped wordline cuts wordline CV^2 ~100x, targeting >10x lower total access energy; on/off ratio and fatigue are the big unknowns.

title: Judo master's leverage: negative-capacitance HZO gate on access transistor
idea: Judo turns the opponent's force against him. A matched ferroelectric HZO layer in the access transistor's gate stack uses its negative-capacitance region to amplify surface potential, reaching ~35 mV/dec over the critical decades, so the same off-current needs a ~0.5 V lower threshold and the wordline swings ~1.2 V straight from the supply.
why: A pumped 3 V swing becoming a direct 1.2 V swing is ~15x less wordline energy per toggle; HZO serves as a gate amplifier, not as the memory element covered in prior work.

title: Ski patrol's avalanche trigger: feedback-FET access switch
idea: Ski patrol releases a whole avalanche with one small charge. The access device is a gated p-i-n-i-n feedback FET whose intrinsic regions are electrostatically doped by the gate; past threshold, injected carriers collapse the internal barriers by positive feedback, giving <1 mV/dec switching at ~0.5 V and a hard barrier when off.
why: A ~0.5 V wordline instead of 3 V cuts wordline CV^2 ~36x with very high on/off, putting total access energy >=10x lower; hysteresis must be tuned so the device releases cleanly.

title: Electrician's circuit breaker: NbO2 threshold film in the access source
idea: A breaker stays open until demand trips it. A thin NbO2 insulator-metal-transition film sits in series with each access transistor's source contact: it stays insulating, blocking subthreshold leakage, until the low-Vt transistor is driven, then snaps metallic, giving an effectively steep slope so the wordline can swing ~1 V.
why: Hyper-FET action drops the wordline from a pumped 3 V to ~1 V (~9x on CV^2, more with no pump) while the insulating film doubles as a leakage blocker; risks are NbO2 off-resistance and threshold drift.

title: Firefly's lantern: photovoltaic row gates driven by waveguide light
idea: A firefly signals with light, not wires. Each electrical wordline becomes a SiN waveguide; per 32-cell segment, a series stack of three nanoscale photodiodes turns a femtojoule light pulse into ~1.5 V of local gate drive, and a shunt pull-down discharges it after the pulse.
why: No long metal wordline is charged from a pump, so gate energy per access falls from pJ to ~fJ optical plus laser wall-plug cost (>=10x), and wordline coupling that drives row hammer disappears.

title: 2050 quantum engineer: superconducting loops with nanowire-cryotron access
idea: A 2050 quantum-computing engineer already has 4 K space to spare. Each bit is a persistent current in a NbN loop, selected by a nanowire cryotron (nTron) that a small gate current drives normal; loops hold current indefinitely, so there is no leakage or refresh, and switching costs attojoules.
why: Device-level access energy drops 100-1000x and refresh is zero; fits as working memory next to cryogenic processors where cooling already exists.

title: Drip-irrigation farmer: 0.5 fF planar cells with virtual-ground sensing
idea: Drip irrigation delivers a few drops where needed instead of flooding the field. An ultra-low-leakage wide-gap access device (off <1e-21 A) lets the capacitor shrink to a planar 0.5 fF, 10x below today's 5 fF pillar, and the bitline is clamped by a virtual-ground charge integrator so the tiny packet lands on a small feedback capacitor without swinging the bitline.
why: Retention stays >1 s with 10x less charge, so charge moved per access falls ~10x and the 60-75:1 pillar (fact 1) and its HAR-etch capital disappear.

title: Wine taster's sip: non-destructive subthreshold current read without restore
idea: A taster sips; she never drains the bottle. The wordline rises only to a subthreshold 'sip' level for ~2 ns; the storage-node voltage modulates the access device's subthreshold current exponentially, and a current-mode sense amp on a bitline held at mid reads it while drawing <1% of stored charge; a per-row read counter triggers a full restore only after ~50 sips.
why: Removes the full bitline swing and destructive-read restore (fact 8) from most reads with a ~1 V sip wordline, cutting read access energy ~10x.

title: Coin collector counts every coin: few-electron Coulomb-blockade cells
idea: A coin collector tracks each coin. Each bit is ~50-200 electrons on a 5 nm silicon or metal nanodot, reached through Coulomb-blockade tunnel junctions of a single-electron access transistor; the island charging energy (>10 kT) blocks leakage, and a ~0.3 V gate swing moves the electrons.
why: Charge per bit drops ~100x from ~30k electrons, and swing to ~0.3 V, so device-level access energy falls ~100x; revisits Hitachi's PLED concept with modern nanodot precision.

title: Burrowing mole's shortcut: heterojunction tunnel-FET access at 0.5 V
idea: A mole tunnels through the hill instead of climbing it. The access device is a vertical Ge-source/Si-channel tunnel FET: band-to-band tunneling turns it on within ~0.3 V at sub-60 mV/dec, and when off the tunneling window closes, leaving no thermionic tail.
why: A ~0.5 V wordline instead of a pumped 3 V cuts wordline energy ~30x; the low on-current is acceptable on short local bitlines, giving >=10x lower access energy.

title: Octopus's arm brains: 3D latch sense amps on 8-cell bitlines
idea: An octopus puts neurons in every arm. A back-end oxide-semiconductor latch sense amp is stacked above every 8-cell vertical bitline segment, so a cell shares charge with ~0.2 fF instead of a ~60 fF, 512-cell bitline, and only a gated global line carries the result out.
why: Bitline charging dominates array energy; cutting bitline load ~100x allows a 0.5 V array with large signals, ~10x lower energy per access, and moves sense amps off the substrate (periphery is ~49% of die, fact 7).

title: Pumped-hydro operator: stepwise tank-capacitor wordline charging
idea: A pumped-hydro plant lifts water in stages and recovers it on the way down. Each wordline driver steps its line through 8 intermediate rails held by shared on-die tank capacitors (0, VPP/8 ... VPP) and steps it down the same way, returning charge to each tank.
why: Stepwise charging divides the CV^2 dissipation by the step count; 8 steps plus fewer pump-supplied coulombs cut wordline energy ~8-12x per access using standard transistors.

title: Chameleon's skin: electro-optic non-destructive readout of stored charge
idea: A chameleon displays its state as color. A thin barium titanate electro-optic layer beside each storage node lets the node voltage shift, via the Pockels effect, the resonance of a micro-ring on a row waveguide; reading a row means shining light through and detecting per-cell resonance shifts, with no bitline swing and no charge removed.
why: Non-destructive optical read removes bitline charging and restore, potentially >=10x lower read energy per bit and no read disturb; density of micro-rings is the major risk.

title: Club bouncer's guest list: cold-source energy-filter access FET
idea: A bouncer admits only the guests on the list. The access transistor gets a 'cold source': a semimetal or superlattice source whose density of states cuts off above a narrow energy window, filtering out the hot Boltzmann-tail electrons behind subthreshold leakage, so slope reaches ~30-40 mV/dec at room temperature.
why: Same leakage at ~0.4 V lower threshold lets a ~1 V wordline run without a pump, ~10-15x lower wordline energy per access, with no ferroelectric or moving parts.

title: Piano tuner's touch: per-cell threshold trim eliminates the wordline pump
idea: A piano tuner adjusts every string. At final test, a thin charge-trap layer in each access transistor's gate stack is programmed by Fowler-Nordheim pulses to center its threshold within +/-15 mV, collapsing the variation margin that forces VPP to ~3 V; the wordline then runs at VDD (1.1 V) directly, with no charge pump.
why: Pumps are ~30% efficient and energy goes as V^2: (3/1.1)^2 x ~3 is ~20x lower wordline energy per access, and the tight threshold spread also removes many tail cells.

title: Postal carrier rings one doorbell: BEOL TFT micro-wordline drivers
idea: A postal carrier rings one doorbell, not the whole building. Oxide-TFT micro-wordline drivers are stacked in the back end over the array, one per 16-cell wordline segment, AND-ing a global row line with a column-group line, so an access charges only 16 cells' gates and swings only 16 bitlines.
why: Wordline and bitline energy per access fall ~32-64x versus a 1k-cell segment, and the drivers take no silicon area (periphery is ~49% of die, fact 7).
